what: Redux keeps the whole app state in one store. You never change it directly: you dispatch an action ({ type: "todo/add" }), and a pure reducer (state, action) => newState computes the next state.
The store has three methods: getState, dispatch and subscribe. On creation it dispatches an @@INIT action so reducers can return their default state.
combineReducers splits state by key, one reducer per slice. applyMiddleware wraps dispatch so code can run between "action sent" and "reducer runs" (logging, async thunks).

steps: createStore: if an enhancer is given, return enhancer(createStore)(reducer, preloadedState).
Keep state and a list of listeners. dispatch(action): check it is a plain object with a type, run the reducer, freeze the new state, call every listener, return the action.
subscribe(fn) adds a listener and returns an unsubscribe function. Dispatch { type: "@@INIT" } at the end of createStore.
combineReducers(map): returns a reducer that calls each slice reducer with state[key] and builds a new object.
applyMiddleware(...mws): create the store, give each middleware { getState, dispatch }, and compose them around the real dispatch: mw(api)(next)(action).
how.diagram:
dispatch(action)
  -> logger(next) -> thunk(next) -> real dispatch
                                       reducer(state, action) -> newState
                                       notify listeners
middleware shape:  store => next => action => { ...; return next(action) }

where: This is the core of Redux; RTK adds helpers on top.
Pure reducers + action logs make replay easy.
React's useReducer is the same reducer idea for one component.
Small apps or server data (use a data-fetching library); a global store adds ceremony.

think.q: Why must a reducer return a new object instead of changing state?
opts: Subscribers (like React) detect changes with ===; mutating keeps the same reference, so nothing updates
Objects cannot be changed in JS
why: Change detection compares references. Same object = "no change".
Pure reducers also make testing and time travel possible.

think.q:
const mw = (name, log) => () => (next) => (action) => { log.push(name); return next(action) }
const log = []
const run = [mw("A", log), mw("B", log)].reduceRight((next, m) => m()(next), () => log.push("reducer"))
run({})
console.log(log.join(" "))
why: Middlewares are composed from the right, so the first one listed is the outermost: it runs first.
Each calls next to pass the action on; the real dispatch is last.

think.q: What does a thunk middleware do with dispatch((dispatch) => …)?
opts: Calls the function with dispatch and getState instead of passing it to the reducer
why: A thunk lets you dispatch later, after an async call finishes.
Without the middleware, the store rejects anything that is not a plain object with a type.

think.q: Why dispatch @@INIT when the store is created?
opts: So each reducer runs once and returns its default state (state = initial argument)
Redux needs at least one action in history
why: Reducers usually look like (state = initial, action). Calling them once with an unknown action fills in those defaults.
No reducer handles @@INIT, so each just returns its default.

watch: How do reducers get their default state?
What is the exact shape of a middleware?
Inside a middleware, which dispatch does api.dispatch call: the raw one or the wrapped one?

reqs: createStore(reducer, preloadedState?, enhancer?) returns { getState, dispatch, subscribe } and dispatches { type: "@@INIT" } at once.
dispatch accepts only plain objects with a type (else throws), runs the reducer, notifies subscribers and returns the action. State is frozen.
subscribe returns an unsubscribe function.
combineReducers gives each reducer its own slice.
applyMiddleware(...mws) is an enhancer; middleware shape is api => next => action, and api.dispatch goes through the whole chain.

what: In Vue, writing state.count++ updates the screen by itself. The trick: reactive(obj) returns a Proxy that notices every read and every write.
While watchEffect(fn) runs fn, every property fn reads is recorded as a dependency. Later, writing one of those properties re-runs fn. Nothing else does.
computed(getter) is a lazy, cached value: it recomputes only when one of its dependencies changed and someone reads .value.

steps: Keep a global activeEffect and a WeakMap: target → Map(key → Set of effects).
Proxy get: if an effect is active, add it to the Set for (target, key) (track). If the value is an object, return reactive(value) too.
Proxy set: if the value really changed, store it and re-run every effect in that Set (trigger).
watchEffect(fn): wrap fn in a runner that first removes itself from its old dependency Sets (cleanup), sets activeEffect, runs fn, then restores the previous active effect. Run it once.
computed(getter): keep dirty = true and a cached value; an inner effect marks it dirty (and triggers readers of .value) when its dependencies change.

where: Solid, Preact signals and Angular signals use the same track/trigger idea.
Observable state that re-runs reactions automatically.
Data you replace as a whole (immutable updates, Redux style) gains little from tracking each property.

think.q:

p.x = 1
p.x++
How many lines are printed?
why: p.x = 1 is one set; p.x++ reads and then sets again: two sets in total.
Every write goes through the trap, which is how changes are detected.

think.q: An effect reads s.ok ? s.a : s.b. s.ok becomes false. Should a later change to s.a re-run it?
opts: It depends on the order of keys
No; on every run, old dependencies are cleared and only what this run read (ok, b) is tracked
why: Dependencies must match the last run. Clean up before each run, then track again.
Without cleanup, effects re-run for values they no longer use.

think.q: s.count = s.count (same value). What should happen?
opts: Nothing: trigger only when the value actually changed (Object.is)
why: Re-running for a no-op write wastes work and can cause loops.
Compare old and new with Object.is before triggering.

think.q: Why is computed lazy (it recomputes only when read)?
opts: Proxies cannot run code on write
If nobody reads it, the work is wasted; marking it dirty is cheap, computing may be expensive
why: Many writes in a row would recompute many times. Dirty-flag plus compute-on-read does it once.
Reading twice without changes returns the cached value.

problems.pseudo:
targetMap = WeakMap(target -> Map(key -> Set(effect)))
activeEffect = null

track(t, k): if activeEffect: deps(t, k).add(activeEffect); activeEffect.deps.push(that set)
trigger(t, k): for e of copy of deps(t, k): e.scheduler ? e.scheduler() : e()

reactive(obj): Proxy(obj, {
  get(t, k, r): v = Reflect.get(t, k, r); track(t, k); return v is object ? reactive(v) : v
  set(t, k, v, r): old = t[k]; Reflect.set(t, k, v, r); if !Object.is(old, v): trigger(t, k); return true })

watchEffect(fn):
  runner(): remove runner from every set in runner.deps; deps = []
            prev = activeEffect; activeEffect = runner; try fn() finally activeEffect = prev
  runner()

computed(getter):
  dirty = true; value
  runner = effect(getter) with scheduler: () => if !dirty: dirty = true; trigger(obj, 'value')
  obj = { get value() { track(obj, 'value'); if dirty: value = runner(); dirty = false; return value } }

What do you do with old dependencies before an effect runs again?
When exactly should a computed value recompute?

reqs: watchEffect(fn) runs fn at once and again whenever a reactive property it read changes.
Only properties read during the last run are dependencies (clean up before re-running).
Writing the same value does not trigger anything.
Nested objects are reactive too.
computed(getter).value is lazy and cached; it updates after its dependencies change and can be used inside effects.

notes: Track on read, trigger on write: the whole system is these two functions plus a Proxy.
activeEffect is how a read knows who is reading. Restore the previous one after each run (effects can nest).
Cleanup before each run keeps dependencies equal to what the last run actually read.
computed = an effect with a scheduler that only marks dirty; it recomputes on read.

problems.signature: h(type, props, ...children) / renderToString(vnode) / diff(oldNode, newNode) / patch(node, patches)

what: A virtual DOM is a plain-object copy of the UI: { type: "li", props: { class: "done" }, children: ["Milk"] }. Building these objects is cheap; touching the real DOM is not.

When state changes you build a new tree and diff it against the old one. The diff is a short list of patches (replace this node, change this prop, insert that child), and only those are applied to the real page.
Here you build the pure core: h to create nodes, renderToString, diff to make patches, and patch to apply them to a tree. Applying the same patches to real DOM nodes is the last small step.

steps: h(type, props, ...children): flatten children, drop null/false/undefined, turn numbers into strings. Text nodes are plain strings.

diff(a, b, path = []): if either is a string, or the types differ → one { type: "REPLACE", path, node: b }. Same element type → compare props (one PROPS patch with set and remove if anything changed), then children.
Children by index: shared indexes → recurse with [...path, i]; extra new children → INSERT at their index; extra old children → REMOVE, highest index first so indexes stay valid.
patch(node, patches): work on a deep copy; for each patch walk the path through children and apply it. The result must equal the new tree.
how.diagram:
old: ul [ li "A", li "B", li "C" ]
new: ul [ li "A", li "X" ]
diff:
  { REPLACE, path [1, 0], node "X" }     text inside the 2nd li
  { REMOVE,  path [],     index 2 }      the 3rd li is gone
patch(old, diff) -> deep-equal to new

where: All diff a virtual tree and patch the real DOM.
renderToString is how the first HTML is made on the server.
Comparing plain trees is easy; comparing real DOM is not.
Svelte and Solid compile to direct DOM updates and skip the diff entirely.

think.q: An element changes from div to section with the same children. What does the diff do?
opts: Compares the children one by one
Replaces the whole subtree with one REPLACE
why: Different types are assumed to be different things, so React-style diffs replace the whole subtree instead of searching for matches.
That rule keeps the diff O(n) instead of very slow general tree matching.

think.q: Why emit REMOVE patches from the highest index down?
opts: Removing index 1 first shifts later children left, so "remove index 3" would hit the wrong child
why: After a removal, every later child moves one index down.
Going from the end keeps the earlier indexes valid.

think.q: You insert a new item at the start of a 100-item list. With index-based diffing, roughly how many patches?
opts: 100 or so: every position looks changed, plus one insert at the end
why: Index 0 now holds the new item, index 1 holds the old item 0, and so on: everything shifts.
This is exactly why React asks for keys: they let the diff match children by identity.

problems.signature: class Observable(subscribeFn) { subscribe, map, filter, take }

what: A promise gives you one value. An observable gives you many values over time (clicks, socket messages, timer ticks), then maybe completes or errors.

new Observable(subscriber => { … }) stores a function that produces values. Nothing happens until someone calls subscribe({ next, error, complete }), and every subscriber gets its own run (it is lazy and cold).
The producer may return a teardown function (clear a timer, remove a listener). unsubscribe() runs it and stops all further values. Operators like map, filter, take return new observables.

steps: Store subscribeFn in the constructor.
subscribe(observer): accept a function (as next) or an object. Create a safe subscriber with a closed flag: next works only while open; error/complete close it and then run the teardown.
Call subscribeFn(safe) inside try/catch (a throw becomes error). Save what it returns as the teardown.
Return { unsubscribe }: close, run the teardown once.
Operators: map(fn) = new Observable that subscribes to this and forwards fn(v); filter forwards only matches; take(n) forwards n values, then completes (which also unsubscribes from the source).
how.diagram:
interval(10).filter(n => n % 2 === 0).map(n => n * 10).take(3)
source:  0  1  2  3  4  5 ...
filter:  0     2     4
map:     0     20    40
take(3): 0     20    40  -> complete -> source timer cleared

where: HTTP, forms and routing in Angular are built on observables.
Debounced search: keyup stream → debounce → switch to a request.
WebSocket messages, price tickers, live notifications.
A single async result: a promise is simpler.

think.q: Two components subscribe to the same (cold) observable that makes an HTTP request. How many requests?
opts: 2: each subscription runs the producer function again
why: Cold observables run their producer per subscriber. That is lazy and simple, but can duplicate work.
Sharing needs a multicast operator (a Subject, share()).

think.q: After complete() is called, the producer calls next(5). What should the subscriber see?

problems.signature: class Scheduler({ maxConcurrent }) { schedule(task, priority), run() }

what: A scheduler decides which job runs next. Jobs have a priority: high, normal or low. Whenever a slot is free, the oldest high job goes first, then normal, then low.
At most maxConcurrent jobs run at the same time. A high job added later still jumps ahead of the low jobs that are waiting (it does not stop jobs that are already running).
schedule(task, priority) returns a promise for that task's result. run() starts processing and resolves when the queues are empty and nothing is running.

steps: Three arrays (queues) for high / normal / low, a running count, and a started flag.
schedule: return a new promise; push { task, resolve, reject } into its queue; if started, call pump().
pump(): while running < maxConcurrent and some queue has a job, take the first job from the highest non-empty queue and start it.
Starting a job: running++, call task(), resolve or reject the job's promise, then running-- and pump() again. If nothing is queued or running, resolve the pending run() promises.
run(): set started, return a promise that resolves when everything is done, and call pump().
how.diagram:
maxConcurrent 1
queues: high [ ]  normal [N1, N2]  low [L1]
run -> N1 starts
while N1 runs: schedule(H1, 'high')  -> high [H1]
N1 done -> pick high first -> H1, then N2, then L1
order: N1 H1 N2 L1

where: React's scheduler runs urgent updates (typing) before low ones (rendering a big list).
Payment jobs before email jobs in a worker.
Visible images first, below-the-fold images later.
If every job matters equally, a plain concurrency limiter is enough.

think.q: maxConcurrent 1. Before run(): schedule L1 (low), N1 (normal), H1 (high), N2 (normal). What is the run order?
why: High first, then normal in the order they were added (FIFO), then low.
Inside one priority, the oldest job wins.

think.q: A low job is running. A high job is scheduled. What happens with this design?
opts: The low job is stopped at once
The low job finishes; the high job runs next, before any other waiting job
The high job waits for all low jobs
why: JavaScript cannot interrupt a running async function from outside.
Priority decides who starts next. Stopping running work needs cooperation (an AbortSignal).

think.q: What is the risk if high jobs keep arriving all the time?
why: Strict priority can starve the lowest queue.
Fixes: aging (raise a job's priority while it waits) or giving low jobs a share of slots.

q.high.push("h1")

problems.pseudo:
class Scheduler({ maxConcurrent = 3 }):
  queues = { high: [], normal: [], low: [] }; running = 0; started = false; waiters = []

  schedule(task, priority = 'normal'):
    return new Promise((resolve, reject) =>
      queues[priority].push({ task, resolve, reject })
      if started: pump())

  pump():
    while running < maxConcurrent:
      job = first job of high, else normal, else low; if none: break
      running++
      Promise.resolve().then(job.task).then(job.resolve, job.reject).finally(() => { running--; pump() })
    if running == 0 and all queues empty: resolve every waiter

  run():
    started = true
    p = new Promise(r => waiters.push(r)); pump(); return p

Where do you start the next job when one finishes?

The next task is always the oldest one in the highest non-empty queue (high, normal, low; default normal).
Never more than maxConcurrent tasks at once (default 3).
schedule returns a promise of that task's result; a failing task rejects only its own promise.
run() resolves when all queues are empty and nothing is running.

notes: Three FIFO queues + "take from the highest non-empty one" = priority scheduling.
Every finished task calls pump() again, so free slots are filled at once.
Each job carries its own resolve/reject, so failures stay isolated.
run() resolves only when nothing is queued and nothing is running.
Strict priority can starve low jobs; aging is the usual fix.

problems.signature: class Container { register(name, factory), singleton(name, factory), resolve(name) }

what: Without dependency injection, a class builds its own helpers: new UserService() calls new Database() inside. That makes it hard to swap the database in tests.

With a container, you register how to build each thing once (register("db", () => new Database())), and code asks for it by name (resolve("db")). Factories receive the container, so they can resolve their own dependencies.

register gives a new instance every time; singleton builds it once and reuses it. A good container also spots circular dependencies (A needs B, B needs A) and explains them instead of overflowing the stack.

steps: Store providers in a Map: name → { factory, singleton, instance }.
register / singleton just save the provider (re-registering replaces it).
resolve(name): unknown name → throw No provider for "name". Singleton already built → return it.
Keep a resolving stack of names being built. If name is already on it → throw Circular dependency: a -> b -> a.
Push the name, call factory(this), pop it in finally (so an error does not leave the stack dirty), cache it if singleton, return it.
how.diagram:
container.singleton('config', () => ({ url: 'db://' }))
container.singleton('db', (c) => new Db(c.resolve('config')))
container.register('users', (c) => new UserService(c.resolve('db')))

resolve('users')  stack: [users]
  resolve('db')   stack: [users, db]
    resolve('config') -> built once, cached
  db built, cached
users built (new one every time)

where: NestJS, Angular and InversifyJS are built around DI containers.
Register a fake mailer in tests, the real one in production.
One place decides which implementation the app uses.
Small apps: passing dependencies as function arguments is DI without a container.

think.q: Why does the factory receive the container as its argument?
opts: So it can resolve its own dependencies without knowing how they are built
why: (c) => new UserService(c.resolve("db")) asks for "db" by name; the container decides what that is.
That is the whole decoupling.

think.q: A singleton depends on a non-singleton (register) service. How many instances of that dependency does the singleton ever see?
opts: A new one on every call to the singleton
Exactly one: the singleton is built once, so its dependency is resolved once
why: The singleton's factory runs once, so the transient dependency is created once for it.
This "captive dependency" surprise is a classic DI bug.

think.q: A resolve throws in the middle (a factory crashed). What must happen to the resolving stack?
opts: Pop the name in finally; otherwise the next resolve of that name wrongly reports a circular dependency
Mark the service as broken forever
why: Without finally, the failed name stays on the stack.
The next resolve would see it and throw a false "Circular dependency".

think.q:
const stack = ["a", "b"]
const name = "a"
console.log("Circular dependency: " + [...stack.slice(stack.indexOf(name)), name].join(" -> "))
why: Slice from where the name first appeared, then add it again to close the loop.
A message with the full path saves a lot of debugging time.

problems.pseudo:
class Container:
  providers = Map(); resolving = []

  register(name, factory):  providers.set(name, { factory, singleton: false })
  singleton(name, factory): providers.set(name, { factory, singleton: true, built: false })

  resolve(name):
    p = providers.get(name); if !p -> throw 'No provider for "name"'
    if p.singleton and p.built -> return p.instance
    if name in resolving:
      cycle = [...resolving from name, name].join(' -> ')
      throw 'Circular dependency: ' + cycle
    resolving.push(name)
    try:
      instance = p.factory(this)
    finally:
      resolving.pop()
    if p.singleton: p.instance = instance; p.built = true
    return instance

How do you detect A → B → A?
What happens to the resolving stack when a factory throws?

reqs: register(name, factory): every resolve calls the factory again (new instance).
singleton(name, factory): built on first resolve, then the same instance forever.
Factories get the container, so they can resolve their own dependencies.
Unknown names throw an error that contains No provider for "name".
Circular dependencies throw Circular dependency: a -> b -> a, and the container keeps working after any error.

checks.verify: const c = new Container(); let msg = ''; try { c.resolve('mailer') } catch (e) { msg = e.message } assert(msg.includes('No provider for "mailer"'), 'message was: ' + msg)

checks.t: Circular dependencies are detected with the path
checks.test:

c.register('b', (k) => k.resolve('a'))
try { c.resolve('a') } catch (e) { console.log(e.message) } // expected: Circular dependency: a -> b -> a
checks.verify: const c = new Container(); c.register('a', (k) => k.resolve('b')); c.register('b', (k) => k.resolve('c')); c.register('c', (k) => k.resolve('a')); let msg = ''; try { c.resolve('a') } catch (e) { msg = e.message } assert(msg.includes('Circular dependency: a -> b -> c -> a'), 'message was: ' + msg)

what: An analytics SDK (like Segment or Mixpanel) records events such as track("signup", { plan: "pro" }) and sends them to a server. Sending one request per event would be slow and wasteful.
So events wait in a queue and are sent in batches: when 25 have piled up, or every 10 seconds, whichever comes first. identify(userId) tags later events with the user.
Networks fail, so a failed send is retried with backoff, and the queue is saved in storage so events survive a page reload or going offline.

steps: createAnalytics({ send, batchSize, flushInterval, storage, retries, retryDelay }): load any saved queue from storage (key analytics-queue).
track(event, props): push { id, event, props, userId, timestamp }, save the queue, and flush if the queue reached batchSize.

flush(): if empty, resolve. Otherwise take a copy of the queue and call send(batch); on failure wait retryDelay * 2 ** attempt and retry. Only after a success remove those events from the queue and save.
Start a setInterval(flush, flushInterval); destroy() clears it. Avoid two flushes at once by reusing the running flush promise.
how.diagram:
track x24      queue: 24  (saved to storage each time)
track #25      queue: 25 -> flush -> send([25 events])
                      fails -> wait 100 -> retry -> ok -> queue: 0
...10s later   interval -> flush whatever is queued

where: Segment, Mixpanel, Amplitude, PostHog SDKs all batch and retry.
Sentry-like SDKs queue errors and send them in the background.
Queue actions while offline, send when the network is back.
Events that must arrive before something else happens (a payment) need a direct request, not a batch.

think.q: Why remove events from the queue only after send succeeds?
opts: If the send fails or the page closes mid-request, the events are still there to retry
why: Removing first and failing later loses data.
The cost is possible duplicates (if a request succeeded but the reply was lost), which is why each event has an id the server can de-duplicate.

think.q: Batch size 25, interval 10 s. A user sends 3 events and then idles. When are they sent?
opts: Within about 10 seconds, by the interval flush
why: Size triggers flush for busy users; the interval makes sure quiet users' events still go out.
Real SDKs also flush on pagehide using navigator.sendBeacon.

think.q: The interval fires a flush while another flush is still waiting for a slow send. Both send the whole queue. What is the problem?
opts: The same events are sent twice
The second flush deletes the queue
why: Both flushes copied the same events.
Keep the running flush promise and return it while one is in progress.

think.q:
const waits = [0, 1, 2].map(a => 100 * 2 ** a)
console.log(waits.join(","))
why: Exponential backoff doubles the wait after each failed attempt.
It gives a struggling server time to recover instead of hammering it.

problems.pseudo:
createAnalytics({ send, batchSize = 25, flushInterval = 10000, storage = null,
                  retries = 3, retryDelay = 100 }):
  queue = load(storage, 'analytics-queue') or []
  userId = null; running = null
  save() = storage?.setItem('analytics-queue', JSON.stringify(queue))

  track(event, props = {}):
    queue.push({ id: unique, event, props, userId, timestamp: Date.now() }); save()
    if queue.length >= batchSize: flush()
  identify(id): userId = id
  flush():
    if running: return running
    if queue empty: return resolved promise
    batch = copy of queue
    running = (async () =>
      for attempt 0..retries:
        try: await send(batch); remove batch ids from queue; save(); return
        catch: if attempt == retries throw; wait retryDelay * 2^attempt
    )().finally(() => running = null)
    return running
  timer = setInterval(() => flush().catch(() => {}), flushInterval)
  destroy(): clearInterval(timer)

What stops two flushes from sending the same events?
What is saved to storage, and when?

build.problem: Build createAnalytics(options) returning { track, identify, flush, destroy }.
reqs: Options: send(batch) → Promise, batchSize (25), flushInterval ms (10000), storage ({ getItem, setItem }, optional), retries (3), retryDelay (100).
track(event, props) queues { id, event, props, userId, timestamp }; identify(userId) applies to later events.
flush() sends all queued events in one send call; nothing is sent for an empty queue; concurrent flushes share one request.
Auto-flush when the queue reaches batchSize and every flushInterval ms; destroy() stops the timer.
Failed sends retry with exponential backoff; events stay queued until a send succeeds; the queue is saved to and restored from storage key analytics-queue.

const a = createAnalytics({ send: async (b) => { sent.push(b) }, flushInterval: 100000 })
a.track('open'); a.identify('u1'); a.track('click', { id: 7 })
await a.flush(); a.destroy()
console.log(sent.length, sent[0].map((e) => e.event + ':' + e.userId)) // expected: 1 ['open:null', 'click:u1']

checks.t: Empty flush sends nothing; the queue empties after success

checks.t: Flushes automatically at batchSize

checks.verify: const sent = []; const a = createAnalytics({ send: async (b) => { sent.push(b.length) }, batchSize: 3, flushInterval: 100000 }); a.track('1'); a.track('2'); assert(sent.length === 0, 'too early'); a.track('3'); await sleep(10); a.destroy(); assert(sent.join() === '3', 'sent ' + sent.join())

checks.t: Flushes on the interval; destroy stops it

checks.t: Retries with backoff; events stay until success
checks.test: // send fails twice, then works -> 3 calls, same batch, queue empties
checks.verify: let calls = 0; const times = []; const t0 = Date.now(); const a = createAnalytics({ send: async (b) => { calls++; times.push(Date.now() - t0); if (calls < 3) throw new Error('503') }, retries: 3, retryDelay: 20, flushInterval: 100000 }); a.track('x'); await a.flush(); assert(calls === 3, 'send called ' + calls + ' times'); assert(times[2] - times[1] >= 30, 'second wait should be about double: ' + times.join(',')); await a.flush(); assert(calls === 3, 'queue should be empty after success'); const b = createAnalytics({ send: async () => { throw new Error('down') }, retries: 1, retryDelay: 5, flushInterval: 100000 }); b.track('keep'); let failed = false; try { await b.flush() } catch (e) { failed = true } b.destroy(); a.destroy(); assert(failed, 'flush should reject after the last retry')

checks.t: Concurrent flushes share one request

checks.verify: let calls = 0; const a = createAnalytics({ send: async () => { calls++; await sleep(30) }, flushInterval: 100000 }); a.track('x'); const p1 = a.flush(); const p2 = a.flush(); await Promise.all([p1, p2]); a.destroy(); assert(calls === 1, 'send called ' + calls + ' times')
checks.gap: Keep the running flush promise and return it if a flush is already in progress.

checks.t: Queue is saved to storage and restored
checks.test: // events tracked with one instance are sent by the next one
checks.verify: const mem = {}; const storage = { getItem: (k) => (k in mem ? mem[k] : null), setItem: (k, v) => { mem[k] = v } }; const a = createAnalytics({ send: async () => { throw new Error('offline') }, storage, retries: 0, flushInterval: 100000 }); a.track('saved', { x: 1 }); a.destroy(); assert(JSON.parse(mem['analytics-queue']).length === 1, 'should save the queue'); const sent = []; const b = createAnalytics({ send: async (batch) => { sent.push(...batch) }, storage, flushInterval: 100000 }); await b.flush(); b.destroy(); assert(sent.length === 1 && sent[0].event === 'saved', 'restored ' + JSON.stringify(sent)); assert(JSON.parse(mem['analytics-queue']).length === 0, 'storage should be emptied after success')

notes: Queue, batch, send: fewer requests, and the server gets events in bulk.
Remove events only after a successful send; give each event an id so the server can drop duplicates.
One running flush at a time stops double sends.
Exponential backoff plus a saved queue survives bad networks and reloads.
Inject send and storage: the SDK stays testable and works in browsers, React Native or Node.

problems.signature: class FeatureFlagClient(flags) { getFlag(key, user, fallback), isEnabled(key, user) } / bucket(userId, key)

what: A feature flag turns a feature on or off without a new deploy: if (flags.isEnabled("new-checkout", user)). The decision comes from data, not code.

Each flag has a default value and a list of rules checked in order; the first rule that matches decides. Rules can target an allowlist of users, conditions on user properties (country is "IN", age > 18), or a percentage rollout.
Rollouts must be deterministic: the same user always lands in the same bucket (0–99), from a hash of userId + flagKey. Raising 10% to 30% keeps the first 10% in and adds more.

steps: bucket(userId, key): hash the string userId + ":" + key to a 32-bit number and take % 100.
Store flags in a Map by key. getFlag(key, user, fallback): missing flag → fallback.
Walk the rules in order. allow: the user id is in the list. if: compare user[attr] with op (eq, neq, in, gt, lt). percent: bucket(user.id, key) < percent.
First match → return its value. No match → the flag's default.
isEnabled(key, user) = getFlag(key, user, false) === true.
how.diagram:
flag "new-checkout": default false
  rules:
   1. allow ["asha"]                 -> true    (staff testing)
   2. if country eq "US"             -> false   (legal hold)
   3. percent 20                     -> true    (20% rollout)
user { id: "bilal", country: "IN" }
   1 no, 2 no, 3: bucket("bilal:new-checkout") = 13 < 20 -> true

where: Ship code dark, turn it on for 1%, then 10%, then everyone.
Turn off a broken feature in seconds.
Permanent per-plan permissions belong in your auth/billing model, not in flags.

think.q: Why use hash(userId + key) instead of Math.random() < 0.2 for a 20% rollout?
opts: A random check gives the same user a different answer on every page load; a hash always gives the same answer
why: Users would see the feature flicker on and off.
A hash makes the decision stable and needs no stored state.

think.q: Why include the flag key in the hash, not just the user id?
opts: So the same users are not always the first 10% of every rollout; each flag gets its own spread
It is required by the hash function
why: With only the user id, user 13 would be in the first slice of every experiment.
Mixing in the key gives an independent bucket per flag.

think.q: Rules in order: (1) if country eq "US" → false, (2) allow ["asha"] → true. Asha is in the US. What does she get?
why: Rules are checked top to bottom and the first match wins.
Order is part of the flag design: put the allowlist first if staff must always see it.

think.q:
const inRollout = (b, p) => b < p
console.log([5, 15, 25].map(b => [inRollout(b, 10), inRollout(b, 30)].join("/")).join(" "))
why: Bucket 5 is in at 10% and still in at 30%. Raising the percentage never removes anyone.
That is why the bucket must be fixed per user and flag.

problems.pseudo:
bucket(userId, key):
  h = 32-bit hash of (userId + ':' + key)   // FNV-1a + mix
  return h % 100

class FeatureFlagClient(flags):
  map = Map(flag.key -> flag)
  matches(rule, user, key):
    if rule.allow   -> rule.allow includes user.id
    if rule.if      -> compare user[rule.if.attr] with rule.if.value using rule.if.op
    if rule.percent -> user.id exists and bucket(user.id, key) < rule.percent
  getFlag(key, user = {}, fallback):
    flag = map.get(key); if !flag -> return fallback
    for rule of flag.rules: if matches(rule, user, key) -> return rule.value
    return flag.default
  isEnabled(key, user) = getFlag(key, user, false) === true
watch: What makes a user's answer stable across page loads?
Which rule wins when two rules match?
What happens for a flag that does not exist?

build.problem: Build bucket(userId, key) and class FeatureFlagClient(flags) with getFlag(key, user, fallback) and isEnabled(key, user).
reqs: A flag is { key, default, rules }; rules are { allow: [ids], value }, { if: { attr, op, value }, value } (ops eq, neq, in, gt, lt) or { percent, value }.
Rules are checked in order; the first match wins; no match → the flag's default; unknown flag → fallback.
bucket(userId, key) is an integer 0–99, the same every time for the same inputs.
Percent rules use bucket(user.id, flagKey) < percent; a user without an id never matches.
isEnabled returns true only when the value is exactly true.

checks.t: First matching rule wins

rules: [{ if: { attr: 'country', op: 'eq', value: 'US' }, value: false }, { allow: ['asha'], value: true }]
// asha in the US -> false

checks.t: bucket is stable, 0-99, and depends on the flag key
checks.test: console.log(bucket('u1', 'beta') === bucket('u1', 'beta')) // expected: true
checks.verify: const b = bucket('user-1', 'beta'); assert(Number.isInteger(b) && b >= 0 && b <= 99, 'bucket must be 0-99, got ' + b); assert(bucket('user-1', 'beta') === b, 'not stable'); let diff = 0; for (let i = 0; i < 200; i++) if (bucket('u' + i, 'flag-a') !== bucket('u' + i, 'flag-b')) diff++; assert(diff > 150, 'the key should change the bucket, only ' + diff + ' differ')
checks.gap: Hash userId + ":" + key to an unsigned 32-bit number and take % 100.

checks.t: Percentage rollout is deterministic, sized right and only grows
checks.test: // 30% rollout over 2000 users -> about 600 enabled; at 50% all of those are still in
checks.verify: const mk = (p) => new FeatureFlagClient([{ key: 'roll', default: false, rules: [{ percent: p, value: true }] }]); const f30 = mk(30); const f50 = mk(50); let on = 0; for (let i = 0; i < 2000; i++) { const u = { id: 'user-' + i }; const a = f30.isEnabled('roll', u); if (a) { on++; assert(f50.isEnabled('roll', u), 'raising the percent removed a user') } assert(f30.isEnabled('roll', u) === a, 'not deterministic') } assert(on > 480 && on < 720, 'expected about 600, got ' + on); assert(f30.getFlag('roll', {}) === false, 'no id should not match a percent rule')
checks.gap: Match when user.id exists and bucket(user.id, flag.key) < rule.percent.

checks.t: isEnabled is strictly true
checks.test:
const ff = new FeatureFlagClient([{ key: 'v', default: 'green', rules: [] }])
console.log(ff.isEnabled('v', { id: 1 })) // expected: false
checks.verify: const ff = new FeatureFlagClient([{ key: 'v', default: 'green', rules: [] }, { key: 'on', default: true, rules: [] }]); assert(ff.isEnabled('v', { id: 1 }) === false, 'a non-boolean value is not enabled'); assert(ff.isEnabled('on', { id: 1 }) === true, 'true flag'); assert(ff.isEnabled('missing', { id: 1 }) === false, 'missing flag')
checks.gap: return this.getFlag(key, user, false) === true.

notes: Rules in order, first match wins, then the default: easy to reason about and to show in an admin UI.
A hash of userId:flagKey gives every user a stable bucket per flag, with no storage.
bucket < percent means raising the percentage only adds users.
Keep evaluation pure and local; fetch the flag definitions from a server separately.
